name: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (consolidated with Trump v. V.O.S. Selections, No. 25-250)
outcome: The Court ruled against the Trump administration, holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize the president to impose tariffs, which struck down both the 'reciprocal' and the drug-trafficking tariffs.
author: Chief Justice Roberts
dissents: Kavanaugh (joined by Thomas and Alito); Thomas also wrote a separate dissent
notes: Disposition: V.O.S. Selections (25-250) affirmed. In Learning Resources (24-1287) the D.C. district court's judgment was vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, because the Court of International Trade has exclusive jurisdiction. Some parts of Roberts's opinion (II-A-2 and III) drew only a plurality. Gorsuch, Barrett and Kagan reportedly wrote concurrences. The Court did not decide refunds of tariffs already paid. One later SCOTUSblog piece was summarized as quoting Alito in a 'separate dissent'; the official lineup has him joining Kavanaugh's dissent.

name: Trump v. Slaughter
outcome: The Court ruled for President Trump, holding that the FTC Act's protection of commissioners against removal except for cause violates the separation of powers and overruling Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935), so the president may fire FTC commissioners at will.
author: Chief Justice Roberts
notes: Reversed and remanded. Thomas joined all of the opinion except Part III-B. Gorsuch concurred. The opinion said it does not decide the status of officials not before the Court, and it left tenure protections for non-Article III judges for another day. This is separate from the September 22, 2025 stay order (25A264), where Kagan wrote the dissent.

name: Trump v. Barbara
outcome: The Court ruled against the Trump administration and struck down Executive Order 14160, holding that children born in the United States to parents who are in the country unlawfully or temporarily are U.S. citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause.
vote: 6-3 on the judgment (5 justices joined the majority opinion's constitutional holding)
author: Chief Justice Roberts
dissents: Thomas (joined by Gorsuch); Alito; Gorsuch (separately). Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment in part and dissented in part.
notes: Affirmed. Sotomayor, Kagan, Barrett and Jackson joined Roberts's opinion. Kavanaugh would have struck down the order only under the citizenship statute, 8 U.S.C. 1401(a), not the Constitution. Jackson concurred, and Sotomayor joined part of that concurrence. Sources count the vote differently, but the facts are the same: SCOTUSblog and NPR say 6-3, counting Kavanaugh with the judgment, while Oyez calls it a 5-4 majority opinion. The order never took effect.

name: Trump v. Cook
outcome: The Court denied the Trump administration's request to let it remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook while her lawsuit continues, holding on narrow grounds that the president did not give Cook the notice and chance to respond that the 'for cause' removal statute requires.
author: Chief Justice Roberts
notes: This was an interim (stay-application) ruling, not a final judgment on the merits: the stay application was denied. Sotomayor, Kagan, Kavanaugh and Jackson joined Roberts. Kavanaugh and Jackson concurred. The Court did not decide whether the mortgage-fraud allegations could be 'cause', or Cook's constitutional due-process claim. It was decided the same day as Slaughter. In August 2026 the administration began a new attempt to remove Cook (CNBC, NBC).

name: Chiles v. Salazar
outcome: The Court sided with Christian counselor Kaley Chiles, holding that Colorado's ban on conversion therapy for minors, as applied to her talk therapy, regulates speech based on viewpoint and must face stricter First Amendment scrutiny than the lower courts applied.
author: Justice Gorsuch
notes: Reversed the Tenth Circuit and remanded. Kagan concurred, joined by Sotomayor, and noted that the Court left open whether a content-based but viewpoint-neutral law would survive. The ruling did not itself strike the law down; the case went back to the lower courts.

name: West Virginia v. B.P.J. (decided together with Little v. Hecox, No. 24-38)
outcome: The Court upheld West Virginia's and Idaho's laws barring transgender girls from girls' and women's school sports teams, holding that the laws violate neither Title IX nor the Equal Protection Clause.
author: Justice Kavanaugh
dissents: Sotomayor (concurring in the judgment in part and dissenting in part, joined by Kagan and Jackson); Jackson (concurring in the judgment in part and dissenting in part)
notes: Thomas and Gorsuch concurred. All three liberal justices agreed that Title IX allows the sex distinction, so some outlets (CNN, Bloomberg Law) call the Title IX holding unanimous; the split was on equal protection. COMPANION CASE: Little v. Hecox (24-38) was decided in the same consolidated opinion (Nos. 24-43 and 24-38). It was NOT dismissed as moot. The Court rejected Hecox's suggestion of mootness, apparently under the voluntary-cessation 'absolutely clear' standard, and reversed and remanded the Ninth Circuit's judgment. Sotomayor's partial dissent said Hecox was moot and focused on B.P.J. The majority's mootness reasoning comes from search snippets of the slip opinion, not a full reading.

name: National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC
outcome: The Court sided with the Republican challengers, holding that federal limits on how much political parties may spend in coordination with their candidates violate the First Amendment.
author: Justice Kavanaugh
notes: The federal government did not defend the limits, so the Court appointed an amicus to defend them. The Court rejected a mootness argument, relying on Vice President Vance's remaining 2028 Senate statement of candidacy. The ruling does not address coordinated-expenditure limits on outside groups. The 2001 Colorado II precedent was treated as no longer controlling.

name: Watson v. Republican National Committee
outcome: The Court upheld Mississippi's law counting mail ballots that are postmarked by Election Day and arrive up to five business days later, holding that the federal Election Day statutes do not require ballots to be received by Election Day.
author: Justice Barrett
dissents: Alito (joined by Thomas and Gorsuch, and by Kavanaugh except Parts II-C-2 and III)
notes: Majority: Barrett, Roberts, Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson. The Court reversed and remanded the Fifth Circuit, which had held that ballots must be received by Election Day. The ruling rests on the statutes, not the Constitution. About 14 states with similar grace periods are affected.

name: United States v. Hemani
outcome: The Court ruled for Ali Hemani, holding that prosecuting him under the federal ban on gun possession by unlawful drug users, based only on his regular marijuana use, violates the Second Amendment as applied to him. It did not strike down the statute itself.
author: Justice Gorsuch
notes: Affirmed the Fifth Circuit. Thomas concurred, arguing the statute may exceed Congress's commerce power. Jackson concurred, joined by Sotomayor. Alito concurred only in the judgment, joined by Kagan, so 7 justices joined the majority opinion. The ruling is narrow: it leaves open disarming drug addicts, people who are intoxicated, and defendants shown individually to be dangerous. One SCOTUSblog 'minutes on the bench' post was summarized as describing a different lineup (an Alito dissent). That conflicts with SCOTUSblog's case page, Oyez and AP-syndicated reports (9-0) and appears to be an error.

name: Cox Communications, Inc. v. Sony Music Entertainment
outcome: The Court ruled for Cox and threw out the billion-dollar verdict for the record labels, holding that an internet provider is contributorily liable for users' copyright infringement only if it intended its service to be used for infringement, by inducing it or by offering a service tailored to it. Failing to cut off known infringers is not enough.
vote: 9-0 on the judgment (7-2 on the reasoning)
author: Justice Thomas
dissents: None (Sotomayor, joined by Jackson, concurred only in the judgment)
notes: Reversed the Fourth Circuit and remanded. Sony's cross-petition on vicarious liability (No. 24-181) was denied. Oyez describes a 7-2 majority opinion and SCOTUSblog a 9-0 judgment; both reflect the same lineup.

name: Chatrie v. United States
outcome: The Court ruled that police use of a geofence warrant to obtain a suspect's Google Location History data was a Fourth Amendment 'search', because people keep a reasonable expectation of privacy in that data. It left open whether this particular warrant was valid and sent the case back to the Fourth Circuit.
vote: 6-3 on the judgment (5-1-3: five joined Kagan's opinion, Gorsuch concurred in the judgment)
author: Justice Kagan
dissents: Alito (joined in part by Thomas and Barrett); Barrett (separately)
notes: Majority opinion joined by Roberts, Sotomayor, Kavanaugh and Jackson. Gorsuch concurred only in the judgment, on a property-based theory. Jackson also concurred. Oyez describes a 5-4 majority opinion and SCOTUSblog 6-3; both reflect the same lineup. The ruling does not ban geofence warrants. One source notes Chatrie's conviction may still stand under the good-faith exception. The exact joins in the dissents come from secondary summaries.

name: Monsanto Co. v. Durnell
outcome: The Court ruled for Monsanto, holding that the federal pesticide law (FIFRA) preempts a Missouri failure-to-warn claim that would have required a cancer warning not on Roundup's EPA-approved label, which threw out a $1.25 million jury verdict for John Durnell.
author: Justice Kavanaugh
notes: Thomas concurred, writing separately about constitutional concerns with FIFRA. Lawyers for plaintiffs say design-defect and other theories may survive. A September 2026 SCOTUSblog preemption commentary was summarized by the search tool as describing an Alito dissent. That conflicts with the opinion, NPR, CNN and SCOTUSblog's news story and is likely a summarizer error or a reference to another case.

name: Hamm v. Smith
outcome: The Court dismissed Alabama's appeal as improvidently granted without deciding how courts should weigh multiple IQ scores, leaving in place the Eleventh Circuit's ruling that Joseph Clifton Smith is intellectually disabled and cannot be executed.
author: None (unsigned one-sentence order dismissing the case as improvidently granted; no majority opinion)
dissents: Alito (joined by Thomas in full and by Roberts and Gorsuch in part); Thomas (separately, urging that Atkins v. Virginia be overruled)
notes: No full merits decision. Sotomayor concurred in the dismissal, joined by Jackson. The question about multiple IQ scores remains open. The vote breakdown (Roberts and Gorsuch joining Alito's dissent in part) comes from summaries of SCOTUSblog's report.

name: Mullin v. Doe (consolidated with Trump v. Miot, No. 25-1084)
outcome: The Court ruled for the Trump administration, holding that the Temporary Protected Status statute bars courts from reviewing non-constitutional challenges to the Homeland Security secretary's decisions to end a country's TPS designation, which allowed the terminations for Syria and Haiti to take effect.
author: Justice Alito
notes: Certiorari before judgment; the case caption changed from Noem to Mullin after Markwayne Mullin became DHS secretary. Roberts, Thomas and Kavanaugh joined Alito in full. Gorsuch and Barrett joined all but Part III-A, a four-justice plurality finding the Haitian plaintiffs' race-based equal-protection claim unlikely to succeed; constitutional claims stay reviewable in principle. Thomas concurred. Reported numbers affected: about 330,000 to 353,000 Haitians and 6,000 to 7,000 Syrians. A UCLA press release gave a June 16 date; the slip opinion and SCOTUSblog give June 25.
